Chapter Three: The Cycle of Violence—Bystanders, Enablers, and the Cost of Silence.
When you think about stories of abuse, you might picture the obvious—the person causing harm, and those who suffer. But what about the ones who see the signs, who hear the shouting, who sense the tension, but simply turn away?
For these sisters, that silence from others—teachers who noticed bruises, neighbors who overheard arguments, even relatives who felt something was off—was almost as painful as the abuse itself.
Their mother was an expert at hiding the truth. She spun stories that painted her as the struggling parent, dealing with “unruly kids” or “ungrateful guests.” And it worked. People bought her act, and the sisters learned, quickly, that asking for help only made things worse.
One time, when one of them tried to confide in an adult she trusted, her mother found out. The punishment that followed sent a crystal-clear message: family loyalty mattered more than honesty. So, the girls became masters at hiding their pain, wearing smiles and pretending everything was fine.
Most of us don’t realize just how easy it is to become a bystander. Maybe you’ve thought, “Someone else will step in,” or “It can’t be as bad as it looks.” But every time someone looked away, it gave the abuse more room to grow. For these sisters, being ignored made them feel invisible—like their suffering was just another family squabble, not something serious.
The mother’s reach didn’t stop at the front door. She managed to manipulate friends, neighbors, even the authorities, convincing them she was just a loving parent doing her best. When social workers came around, she put on a show—always blaming the girls for any trouble. The sisters, terrified of what might happen if they spoke up, stayed quiet.
Over time, the girls started to see just how powerful silence could be. It was almost as if people would rather ignore something uncomfortable than face the truth. And it became clear: breaking this cycle would take more than bravery. It would take someone willing to truly listen—and to believe.
The cost of all that silence? It was steep. The sisters stopped believing adults could help. Instead, they learned to lean on each other, finding comfort in the smallest gestures—a shared smile, a gentle touch, a whispered promise to keep going. These moments became their lifeline.
As the mother’s cruelty only grew, the girls saw her invent new ways to punish and control. Sometimes, even guests in their home suffered, and the sisters were powerless to stop it. The cycle just kept repeating—over and over—with each new person who entered their lives.
Still, in those darkest moments, hope lingered. They dreamed about the day when someone would finally see past the lies, when the truth would come out. No matter what, they promised each other, they’d survive.
So, the next time you wonder how abuse can go unnoticed, remember this: it thrives in silence. It takes real courage to speak up, to risk everything for a shot at freedom. For these sisters, telling their story would change everything—but it would also come at a heavy price.
